title: The Inverse is a Polynomial in A over a Commutative Ring
description: Removes the field hypothesis from the parent inverse-as-polynomial result: over an arbitrary commutative ring R, if the determinant is a unit (IsUnit (det A), strictly stronger than det A ≠ 0), then A⁻¹ = (aeval A) r for the explicit polynomial r = C (Ring.inverse (−c₀)) · divX (charpoly A) of degree < n, where c₀ = (charpoly A).coeff 0. The field inverse (−c₀)⁻¹ is replaced by Ring.inverse (−c₀), the key step being that IsUnit (det A) forces IsUnit (−c₀) via det A = (−1)ⁿ c₀. The witnessing non-field case is GL(n, ℤ): an integer matrix with det = ±1 has an integer-coefficient polynomial inverse, out of reach of the field-only parent. Directly answers the parent oq-07 open question.

meta.assumptions: 0 axioms, 0 sorries. #print axioms reports only [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. The base ring R is an arbitrary commutative ring; the matrix determinant is assumed to be a unit (IsUnit (det A)), which over a general ring is strictly stronger than det A ≠ 0 and is exactly what invertibility requires. The degree-bound and existence theorems additionally assume Nontrivial R and Nonempty n (a 0×0 matrix, or the trivial ring, degenerates the charpoly degree). Built on Mathlib's Cayley–Hamilton and nonsingular-inverse theory.

overview.historicalContext: The parent entry expresses the inverse of an invertible matrix as a polynomial in the matrix, but only over a field, where 'invertible' coincides with 'nonzero determinant'. Over a general commutative ring the two notions split: a matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is a unit of the ring, a strictly stronger condition than being nonzero (in ℤ, det = 2 is nonzero but not a unit, and the matrix has no integer inverse). The classical Cayley–Hamilton division argument nonetheless goes through verbatim once one replaces the field inverse of the scalar −c₀ by Ring.inverse and supplies the fact that a unit determinant makes −c₀ a unit. This yields the inverse-as-polynomial corollary in its natural generality — over ℤ it produces the integer-coefficient inverse of any matrix in GL(n, ℤ).
overview.problemStatement: Generalize the inverse-as-polynomial result from a field to a commutative ring R: show that for A : Matrix n n R with IsUnit (det A), the inverse A⁻¹ = (aeval A) r for an explicit r of degree < n, replacing det A ≠ 0 by IsUnit (det A) and the field inverse (−c₀)⁻¹ by Ring.inverse (−c₀).
overview.text: Let p = charpoly A and c₀ = p.coeff 0. Cayley–Hamilton gives p(A) = 0; peeling off the constant term via p = divX(p)·X + C c₀ and evaluating at A yields (divX p)(A)·A = (−c₀)•1. Since det A = (−1)ⁿ c₀ and det A is a unit, −c₀ is a unit, so multiplying by Ring.inverse (−c₀) exhibits A⁻¹ = Ring.inverse(−c₀) • (divX p)(A) = (aeval A)(C(Ring.inverse(−c₀))·divX p), of degree < n. Hence A⁻¹ ∈ R[A].
overview.proofStrategy: The one new ingredient over the parent is isUnit_neg_charpoly_coeff_zero: from det A = (−1)ⁿ c₀ (Matrix.det_eq_sign_charpoly_coeff) and the fact that (−1)ⁿ is its own inverse, c₀ = (−1)ⁿ det A is a product of units, so IsUnit c₀ and hence IsUnit (−c₀). Everything else ports the parent's field proof by swapping the field division inv_mul_cancel₀ for Ring.inverse_mul_cancel on the unit −c₀. The additive Cayley–Hamilton identity, the promotion of the left inverse via Matrix.inv_eq_left_inv, the degree bound via natDegree_C_mul_le and degree_divX_lt, and the subalgebra membership via Algebra.adjoin_singleton_eq_range_aeval are all valid over a commutative ring unchanged.
keyInsights: Over a commutative ring, invertibility of A is IsUnit (det A), strictly stronger than det A ≠ 0; this is the correct hypothesis and it is exactly what the proof needs
det A = (−1)ⁿ c₀ transfers the unit from the determinant to the constant term of the characteristic polynomial, and (−1)ⁿ being its own inverse makes this a clean two-line argument
The field division (−c₀)⁻¹ is replaced by Ring.inverse (−c₀); Ring.inverse_mul_cancel supplies the cancellation exactly when −c₀ is a unit
The construction is genuinely more general: over ℤ it gives the integer-coefficient inverse of any GL(n, ℤ) matrix, which the field-only parent cannot express since ℤ is not a field
The polynomial inverse coincides with Mathlib's adjugate formula A⁻¹ = Ring.inverse (det A) • adjugate A — two descriptions of one and the same nonsingular inverse

conclusion.summary: Removing the field hypothesis from the parent, the inverse of a matrix over an arbitrary commutative ring with unit determinant is the evaluation at A of an explicit polynomial of degree < n, and lies in the subalgebra R[A]. The single new ingredient is that IsUnit (det A) forces IsUnit (−c₀); the rest of the Cayley–Hamilton division argument ports unchanged with Ring.inverse in place of field division. All 9 theorems and 1 definition are fully verified with 0 sorries and 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: The result holds in its natural generality: over ℤ it produces the integer-coefficient inverse of any GL(n, ℤ) matrix, over polynomial rings the polynomial inverse of a matrix with unit-determinant entries, and so on — none of which the field-only parent can express. It also confirms that the correct notion of invertibility over a commutative ring is IsUnit (det A), matching Mathlib's adjugate-based nonsingular inverse.
